doc.title: Pete Levin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Never seeking work, and Gil Evans and Mulligan as pure artists
summary: Levin says work comes by word of mouth, admits doing jobs for money, and admires pure artists like Gil Evans.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: Yeah, that phone better keep ringing to make that happen, right?

Which is okay, it always has, there were very few periods that I can remember where I was really hurting for work. And in honesty I think I’m very fortunate but for the most part I’ve never gone looking for work, it’s been word of mouth and the phone usually rings. It’s good. I am very fortunate. And I’m still doing stuff now, but looking back I think I’ve spent a lot of time doing things that — okay I really did that one for the money. Somebody was asking me about something just this weekend. I was sitting at a bar and this guy says, “I remember this project that you did, you remember that thing we did—” and I didn’t remember what it was. And I mean I remembered doing it but I didn’t remember anything about it. And why this guy remembered.
Well it made a big impression on him but not on you I guess.

Well it’s a job. And I enjoyed it while I was doing it. It distracts from things that you might like to do. And I’ve worked with several people over the years that I really think of as pure artists. Gil Evans is one, Gerry Mulligan, people who just — I’m going to do this, this is what I do. Gil was constantly turning down offers for professorships. He just said no, I don’t want to do that, I’ve got a gig Monday night playing at Sweet Basil’s. I can’t be up in Massachusetts. So that’s it. Nice to strive for that. I can’t do that. I can’t be a pure artist. I learned that a long time ago. But it’s a thing to admire and it’s a nice thing to at least model part of your life after.
